strengths: Well-motivated task formulation: The proposed OmniDenseCaptioning task addresses a critical gap between global audio-visual captioning (which lacks temporal boundaries) and traditional dense video captioning (which largely ignores auditory context and cinematographic aspects). The 6-dimensional schema provides a comprehensive, script-like representation.

Carefully curated benchmark: OmniDCBench contains 1,122 human-annotated videos with deep and detailed multi-scene annotations (averaging ~995 words per video), establishing a valuable testbed for the community.

Thoughtful metric design: SodaM addresses the boundary ambiguity inherent in scene-level segmentation by using dynamic programming for IoU alignment and merging many-to-one predictions, while reducing the evaluation cost from O(MN) to O(K) LLM-judge calls.

Effective training methodology and strong empirical results: The two-stage training scheme combining SFT with GRPO directly optimizes temporal accuracy and dense captioning quality. The resulting 7B model outperforms strong proprietary models (such as Gemini-2.5-Pro) on the benchmark and shows impressive transferability to downstream VideoQA (Daily-Omni, WorldSense) and temporal grounding (Charades-STA).
weaknesses: Lack of meta-evaluation for SodaM: The CheckList score component of SodaM relies on an LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-Flash) to evaluate atomic fact coverage. The paper lacks a human agreement study (e.g., Pearson/Spearman correlation between SodaM scores and expert human rankings) to rigorously validate the reliability of this automated evaluation metric.

Potential vulnerability to over-generation in many-to-one merging: SodaM concatenates predicted captions when multiple segments match a single ground-truth segment and evaluates atomic recall. This could inadvertently reward models that over-segment and produce redundant text, as there is no explicit precision/penalty metric within SodaM itself (beyond the length reward used during GRPO).

Dependency on closed-source LLMs in the data pipeline: The 42K training set was synthesized using Gemini-2.5-Pro, and evaluation also leverages Gemini models. While OmniDCBench is human-annotated, further analysis on potential stylistic biases or distillation artifacts would strengthen the claims.

Minor presentation and editorial issues: The URL at the end of the Abstract is missing ('publicly available at \n 1'); typographical errors are present (e.g., 'Auiod-Visual Events' in Figure 1 caption, 'exsit-ing' on page 3); and inconsistent model naming occurs between the main text ('Gemini-2.5-Flash') and Table 9 ('Gemini-2-Flash').

strengths: Compelling task formulation: Expanding dense video captioning into an 'Omni Dense Captioning' problem with a structured six-dimensional schema (audio-visual events, background, camera state, shot editing, dialogue, acoustics) provides a rich, script-like representation that bridges video understanding and multimodal generation.

Valuable human-annotated benchmark: OmniDCBench introduces 1,122 meticulously human-annotated multi-scene video samples with rich descriptions (averaging ~995 words per video), establishing a solid testbed for future research.

Principled evaluation metric (SodaM): The proposed SodaM metric addresses key challenges in evaluating continuous scene dense captioning by combining IoU-based dynamic programming alignment, many-to-one segment merging to mitigate boundary ambiguity, and CheckList keypoint scoring.

Effective RL-based training framework: Using GRPO with task-specific rewards (format, length, IoU, and caption quality) effectively combats the severe token imbalance between sparse timestamp tokens (~0.7%) and lengthy descriptive text (~99.3%), leading to measurable improvements over standard SFT.

Extensive downstream validation: The authors demonstrate practical downstream value by using the generated captions to achieve strong performance on multimodal QA benchmarks (Daily-Omni, WorldSense) and fine-tuning transfer on temporal grounding (Charades-STA).
weaknesses: Baseline fairness on format following: In Table 1, general open-source MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-Omni, MiniCPM-o-2.6) score extremely low on SodaM (1.8 to 6.9). Because zero-shot models often struggle with complex multi-field JSON schema formatting rather than visual-audio perception per se, providing few-shot prompting or light SFT baselines would offer a fairer assessment of their true perceptual differences.

Lack of human correlation validation for the metric: SodaM employs Gemini-2.5-Flash as an automated judge for atomic keypoint recall. The paper lacks a quantitative human agreement study (e.g., Pearson/Spearman correlation with human experts) to verify that the LLM-judge checklist scores faithfully mirror human quality assessments.

Direct optimization of the evaluation metric in RL: The GRPO stage uses the exact SodaM metric as the caption reward ($R_C$). While optimizing the target metric is standard in RL, this confers a direct structural advantage on SodaM evaluations; further discussion and analysis regarding potential reward hacking or verbosity bias would strengthen the evaluation.

Temporal scope and video length limitations: As acknowledged in the limitations, the framework primarily operates on short video clips (~50–60 seconds, with training segments cut to 3 minutes or less). Extending this to long-form multi-scene videos currently relies on independent segment-then-caption slicing, which risks losing cross-scene narrative coherence.

strengths: Well-motivated task formulation: Proposing Omni Dense Captioning extends conventional dense video captioning to comprehensive audio-visual-cinematographic dimensions (events, background, camera state, editing style, dialogue, acoustics), creating structured 'script-like' video narratives.

Valuable human benchmark (OmniDCBench): The construction of a 1,122-video human-annotated benchmark with fine-grained multi-dimensional descriptions (averaging ~995 words per video) provides an impactful evaluation suite for the community.

Principled evaluation metric (SodaM): SodaM smartly tackles the multi-granularity scene segmentation mismatch between predictions and ground truth using dynamic programming temporal alignment and many-to-one merging, while significantly lowering LLM judge evaluation complexity.

Comprehensive experimental validation: TimeChat-Captioner-7B demonstrates consistent improvements on the target benchmark, outperforming open-source baselines and competitive proprietary models like Gemini-2.5-Pro, and shows transferable gains on downstream Omni-VideoQA (Daily-Omni, World-Sense) and temporal localization (Charades-STA).
weaknesses: Potential LLM-judge bias and circularity: The training dataset (TimeChatCap-42K) is distilled from Gemini-2.5-Pro, the caption checklist evaluation metric uses Gemini-2.5-Flash as a judge, and the downstream VideoQA evaluation relies on feeding captions into Gemini-2.5-Pro. This heavy reliance on the Gemini family across data generation, evaluation, and downstream QA risks systemic style and evaluation bias.

Unclear online reward implementation in GRPO: The RL stage utilizes SodaM as the caption reward (R_C), which requires Checklist Score computation via an LLM judge. The paper does not adequately detail the compute/latency overhead of running an LLM judge online across 2,000 samples with 8 rollouts each (16,000 judge queries), or whether a surrogate/offline evaluator was used.

Limited temporal scope: Although framed around multi-scene video scripting, the model is trained primarily on short clips (averaging 50–60 seconds, Figure 5a), relying on an unverified segment-then-caption heuristic for longer videos without evaluating potential error propagation across boundaries.

Presentation and citation errors: There are several missing author names in textual citations (e.g., 'IoU (2018)' on page 4, 'GRPO (2025)' on page 7), alongside occasional typos in figures (e.g., 'Qwen-3-Omini' in Figure 4 and 'Auiod-Visual' in Figure 1 caption).

strengths: Well-motivated task formulation: The paper introduces Omni Dense Captioning, addressing key limitations of existing video captioning methods by requiring temporally continuous scene segmentation coupled with structured, six-dimensional audio-visual descriptions (events, background, camera state, shot editing, dialogue, and acoustic cues).

High-quality benchmark and robust evaluation metric: OmniDCBench provides 1,122 expert human-annotated samples. Furthermore, the proposed SodaM metric addresses scene boundary ambiguity via dynamic programming alignment and merging, showing strong human alignment (77.9% case-level agreement) and consistency across four independent LLM judges (Kendall's W = 0.925).

Effective training methodology: Combining SFT with GRPO directly mitigates the timestamp-caption token imbalance and scene boundary ambiguity, utilizing verifiable and metric-aligned rewards (format, length, temporal IoU, and SodaM).

Comprehensive and convincing experimental validation: TimeChat-Captioner-7B outperforms strong open-source models and Gemini-2.5-Pro on OmniDCBench, demonstrates strong transferability on downstream caption-based VideoQA (Daily-Omni, WorldSense) and temporal grounding (Charades-STA), and generates captions that match proprietary models in supervising downstream models.
Thorough ablation and validation studies: The manuscript provides extensive analyses on SFT scaling, reward ablation, DP merging necessity, judge robustness, and hyperparameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: Evaluation metric primarily emphasizes recall: The SodaM CheckList judge evaluates whether ground-truth keypoints are covered by the generated caption. While the length reward regularizes verbosity, the metric lacks an explicit precision/hallucination penalty for generating fabricated visual or acoustic details.

Reliance on proprietary LLM-synthesized training data: The 42K training dataset relies entirely on Gemini-2.5-Pro generations. While the test benchmark is human-annotated, synthetic training data may inherit subtle stylistic and perceptual artifacts from the teacher model.

Scalability limitations on extended video lengths: Due to the 32K context window and dense token requirements (interleaved audio-visual tokens plus lengthy outputs), processing videos longer than a few minutes requires heuristic clip splitting rather than end-to-end continuous modeling.
Minor presentation omissions: In Section D.2, a placeholder appears incomplete ('We recruited approximately annotators through crowdsourcing platforms').

strengths: Formulates a well-motivated and comprehensive omni-modal dense video captioning task covering six structural cinematographic and audio-visual dimensions.
Introduces OmniDCBench, a valuable human-annotated benchmark with detailed segmentations and rich script-like captions.
Proposes the SodaM metric with dynamic programming alignment to resolve temporal boundary ambiguities and granularity mismatches.
Demonstrates strong empirical gains using GRPO post-training, validating transferability to downstream VideoQA and temporal grounding tasks.
weaknesses: Evaluation and reward computation heavily depend on proprietary LLM judges (Gemini-2.5-Flash), which may introduce subtle evaluation biases and high computational costs.
The synthetic training data (TimeChatCap-42K) relies entirely on Gemini-2.5-Pro prompting, potentially bounding the model's performance to the teacher model's capabilities and stylistic distribution.
Context length constraints (32K tokens) restrict end-to-end processing of long-form videos, requiring a clip-level segment-then-caption workaround.

strengths: Addresses the underexplored challenge of joint audio-visual dense captioning across structured semantic dimensions.
Introduces OmniDCBench, providing human-annotated multi-scene video descriptions across six cinematic and audio-visual dimensions.
Presents the SodaM metric to mitigate segment granularity mismatch via dynamic programming alignment, supported by human agreement analyses.
Achieves competitive empirical results against several open-source and proprietary multimodal baselines across dense captioning and downstream VideoQA tasks.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on synthetic training data generated by proprietary LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro), which may inherit biases and limit real-world fidelity.
Potential evaluation circularity, as LLM-based judges evaluate predictions generated by models trained on LLM-synthesized descriptions.
The DP-merging mechanism in SodaM may obscure fine-grained boundary segmentation errors by agglomerating multiple short predictions into a single segment.
Evaluation is predominantly restricted to short clips (<70s), with limited demonstration of scalability to complex long-form video content.
